strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck in joint speech-text modeling: the substantial sequence-length mismatch between speech and text tokens.
TASTE offers an intuitively appealing design that uses an ASR-initialized cross-attention aggregator and residual vector quantization to produce speech representations aligned with transcript tokens.
The reported reconstruction results are promising in bitrate efficiency: TASTE obtains strong WER and estimated naturalness at a substantially lower reported bitrate than the codec baselines.

The evaluation considers both reconstruction and downstream spoken-language-modeling behavior, including acoustic and semantic benchmarks, and explores discrete-token and continuous-embedding variants.
Adapting a text LLM using LoRA is practically attractive, and the reported improvements over the authors' S3-token baseline are substantial.
weaknesses: The central claim that TASTE is a speech tokenizer is overstated because tokenization requires the transcript, while reconstruction additionally receives the transcript and an external speaker embedding. The method therefore does not demonstrate that its tokens independently retain the information attributed to them. In particular, speaker similarity is nearly identical for TASTE and the text-only baseline when both receive speaker conditioning.

The reconstruction comparisons are not well controlled. TASTE is conditioned on text and speaker information and uses CosyVoice-derived units and a pretrained vocoder, whereas several codec baselines operate without speaker embeddings. Consequently, the bitrate-quality comparison is not apples-to-apples, and the bitrate calculation itself is not specified sufficiently to verify the reported approximately 190 bps value.

Important algorithmic details are ambiguous or inconsistent. The appendix defines averaging and alignment only for continuous embeddings, but the main text assumes aligned discrete RVQ indices; it is unclear whether quantization happens before or after word-level averaging. The exact integration of text and speech inputs in TASLM, autoregressive ordering, inference procedure, and handling of generated word boundaries are also insufficiently described.

The downstream evidence is too limited for the broad claims. Evaluation consists mainly of likelihood-based SALMON and StoryCloze accuracy, with no assessment of generated-speech naturalness, intelligibility, prosody, continuation quality, or human preference. Despite efficiency claims, no measured training speed, inference latency, memory use, or FLOP comparison is provided.

Comparisons with prior spoken language models are not controlled for training data, model scale, architecture, or optimization, and no significance estimates or repeated-run variability are reported. The very weak S3 baseline, near chance on SALMON, is not investigated, making it difficult to know whether TASTE's gain reflects the proposed alignment or baseline implementation choices.

Ablations needed to validate the contribution are absent, including tests of the shallow-value cross-attention design, ASR initialization, number and size of RVQ codebooks, word-level averaging, transcript quality, speaker conditioning, and reconstruction objective. Robustness to ASR errors is especially important because transcripts are required at inference.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. UTMOS exceeding ground-truth audio does not establish superior perceptual quality, and similar performance between two model variants is described as demonstrating generalizability without evaluation across datasets, languages, domains, or model families.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the SLM training dataset allocation, number of steps or epochs, loss weights, sampling and decoding procedure, architecture of added input/output modules, parameter counts, preprocessing, and many evaluation details are missing. No code, checkpoints, or audio samples are identified.

The claim of requiring no explicit word alignment is misleading because the LLM adaptation procedure explicitly groups ASR and LLM tokens by words. The paper also lacks discussion of privacy, consent, voice cloning risks, and biases associated with large web-sourced speech data.

strengths: The core idea—making acoustic representations follow the text-token sequence length—is relevant and could substantially reduce the cost of joint speech-text modeling.
The proposed system combines ASR initialization, text-conditioned aggregation, residual vector quantization, and a reconstruction decoder in a coherent architecture.

On LibriTTS test-clean, TASTE achieves favorable automatic reconstruction results at a reported bitrate of approximately 190 bits/s, including 3.8% WER and strong speaker and emotion consistency relative to the text-only baseline.

The resulting 1B TASLM models improve substantially over the paper's S3-token baseline and are competitive with several larger, fully fine-tuned prior systems on the selected SALMON and StoryCloze evaluations.
The paper evaluates both discrete-token and continuous-embedding variants, which produce broadly consistent downstream results.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence is not sufficiently rigorous for a top-tier acceptance. Reconstruction is evaluated only with automatic proxies; there is no human listening study, preference test, intelligibility MOS, or released audio evidence. The claim of high-quality generation is therefore weakly supported.

The reported bitrate comparison is not fully comparable. TASTE reconstruction additionally requires text tokens and a speaker embedding, but their information cost is excluded, while baselines use different conditioning and decoder configurations. UTMOS exceeding the ground-truth score also illustrates metric or vocoder bias rather than evidence that reconstruction surpasses real speech.

The spoken-language-model evaluation contains only likelihood-based discrimination tasks. It does not evaluate generated speech for naturalness, intelligibility, semantic coherence, prosody, diversity, or speaker preservation, despite generation being a central motivation and claim.

Comparisons with prior SLMs are poorly controlled because model sizes, training data, optimization, tokenizers, and fine-tuning regimes differ. The only in-house baseline is an insufficiently described S3-token system that performs near chance on several SALMON dimensions. There is no matched LoRA baseline using another compact tokenizer, nor a full-fine-tuning TASTE comparison.

Essential ablations are absent: shallow versus final encoder values, ASR initialization, word-level averaging, RVQ depth and codebook size, transcript conditioning, speaker embedding, and tokenizer versus embedding modeling. Consequently, the proposed mechanism is not isolated from the many pretrained components inherited from Whisper and CosyVoice.

Robustness to ASR errors is not tested, even though TASTE requires a transcription as tokenizer input. Evaluation is limited to clean read speech for reconstruction, leaving noisy, spontaneous, accented, multilingual, and out-of-domain speech unexamined.

Several technical descriptions are incomplete or inconsistent. Algorithm 1 aligns only continuous embeddings and does not explain how discrete RVQ indices are aggregated at the word level. Equation 13 omits the text next-token loss for the embedding model, and the claimed weighted tokenizer objective is written without weights. Codebook learning and latent inference are also underspecified.

Claims of computational efficiency are not backed by measured training throughput, inference latency, memory use, sequence lengths, or end-to-end cost. A shorter representation alone does not establish the stated system-level savings.

Results lack uncertainty estimates, significance testing, and exact evaluation sample counts. Custom emotion- and duration-consistency metrics are not validated, and reliance on a single off-the-shelf emotion classifier makes the paralinguistic conclusions fragile.

Reproducibility is limited: the SLM training duration or number of updates and precise training-data construction are not reported; several preprocessing, likelihood-scoring, and generation details are missing; and no code, checkpoints, or samples are identified.

The novelty relative to text-conditioned acoustic representations and CosyVoice-style supervised semantic tokens is not convincingly established. Much of the system is assembled from existing ASR, RVQ, speech-unit, vocoder, and LoRA components, while the specialized aggregation change receives no ablation.

The paper contains no substantive limitations, ethics, or misuse discussion despite training on large web-collected speech and enabling speech or voice generation, raising unaddressed concerns about consent, privacy, impersonation, and dataset bias.

strengths: TASTE addresses an important bottleneck in spoken language modeling: the substantial sequence-length mismatch between speech and text tokens. Aligning speech representations to text-token length is intuitive, potentially useful, and computationally attractive.

The proposed tokenizer is technically interesting, combining an ASR-initialized encoder/aggregator, cross-attention to shallow acoustic features, residual vector quantization, and reconstruction training.

The reconstruction results are promising. TASTE reports strong intelligibility and estimated naturalness at a substantially lower nominal bitrate than the evaluated codec baselines, while retaining more emotion and duration information than the text-only condition.

The downstream experiments cover both acoustic sensitivity through SALMON and semantic reasoning through spoken StoryCloze. TASLM substantially improves over the authors' S3-token baseline and is reasonably competitive with several substantially trained prior SLMs despite using LoRA.
The paper is generally understandable, and its figures communicate the tokenizer and language-modeling pipelines effectively.
weaknesses: The nominal bitrate comparison is not fully fair. TASTE reconstruction is additionally conditioned on the ground-truth transcript and a speaker embedding, but the bitrate of this side information is not counted. Competing codecs in the no-speaker-embedding group solve a harder standalone reconstruction problem. The strong text-only baseline further shows how much reconstruction quality comes from these side channels.

The paper lacks the critical ablations needed to attribute gains to text alignment or the proposed architecture. Missing comparisons include standard versus shallow-value cross-attention, ASR initialization, word-level averaging, different RVQ depths, transcript corruption, and a duration-matched or aggressively downsampled codec baseline.

Downstream comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. The only same-training-pipeline baseline, S3-token LoRA, is near chance on SALMON, while prior systems differ in model size, training data, tokenizers, and optimization. There is no full-finetuned TASLM, matched text-aligned alternative, or controlled sequence-length baseline supporting the claim that alignment enables parameter-efficient adaptation.

The empirical coverage is narrower than the claims suggest. Generated speech is not evaluated with human listening tests, continuation quality metrics, diversity measures, or qualitative examples. UTMOS exceeding ground-truth speech should not by itself be interpreted as evidence of superior perceptual quality.

Important evaluation details are missing, particularly how discrete and continuous TASLM variants compute comparable likelihoods on SALMON and StoryCloze. Uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, and significance tests are also absent, making small differences difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the SLM training duration or number of updates, loss weights, several decoder and alignment details, and code or checkpoints are not provided. The paper also does not discuss privacy, consent, voice-cloning misuse, or other ethical issues associated with large-scale web speech and speech generation.

strengths: TASTE presents a clear and practically motivated idea: compress speech into text-aligned tokens so a pretrained text LLM can jointly model lexical and paralinguistic information without long speech-token sequences.

The reported reconstruction results are promising: at approximately 150 bps, TASTE achieves strong predicted quality, speaker similarity, and human MUSHRA scores relative to substantially higher-rate codecs.

The evaluation is broad, covering reconstruction, localized speech editing, continuation, SALMON, StoryCloze, and spoken question answering. The 1.3B TASLM models compare favorably with several larger spoken-language models, especially on continuation and StoryCloze.

The paper is generally understandable, includes useful diagrams and appendices, and discloses datasets, major model components, optimization settings, human-evaluation instructions, and result variability.
weaknesses: The central claim that text alignment itself improves spoken-language modeling is not isolated experimentally. The S3 baseline is insufficient: controlled comparisons against fixed-rate or equally compressed tokens using the same architecture, data, decoder, parameter budget, and training procedure are needed, as are ablations of the aggregator, word-level averaging, RVQ depth, and text-conditioned reconstruction.

The claimed efficiency benefit is not directly evaluated. There are no measurements of training or inference throughput, memory, latency, context utilization, or streaming behavior against padding, interleaving, or delayed-generation alternatives.

The approximately 150-bps comparison is potentially misleading because TASTE reconstruction also requires the transcript and a global speaker embedding, whereas conventional codecs encode speech without such side information. The paper does not state whether these costs are included or provide a rate-distortion comparison under matched conditioning.

Several evaluations inherently supply ASR-derived text alongside speech. StoryCloze and spoken QA may therefore primarily measure an ASR-plus-text-LLM pathway rather than speech representation quality. Likelihood computation, normalization, and comparability for discrete-token versus continuous-embedding models are also insufficiently specified.

The continuation evidence is overstated as showing significant superiority. Only 20 samples per method are used for human evaluation, no confidence intervals or hypothesis tests are reported, and the listed standard deviations appear to describe sample dispersion rather than uncertainty. Against the matched 1B cascade, TASLM's GPT-4o score is essentially tied and its UTMOS score is slightly lower; the small human-score difference is unsupported statistically.

The MUSHRA protocol omits the standard low-pass anchor, uses a small sample set, and conflates quality and similarity. Predicted MOS values exceeding ground truth further illustrate why the objective metrics should not support strong perceptual-quality claims by themselves.

There is a technical inconsistency in the KL objective: for a Gaussian parameterized by standard deviation sigma, the KL term should contain sigma squared, whereas Equation 7 contains sigma while subtracting log sigma squared. It is unclear whether this is a notation error or reflects the implementation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: aggregator and unit-decoder architecture details, the shallow Whisper layer choice, loss weights, spoken-LM training duration, sampling settings, likelihood scoring details, few-shot QA protocol, and statistical-analysis procedures are missing. The manuscript's code/demo links are also blank in the supplied PDF.

The method depends on ASR transcripts and non-streaming processing, limiting its applicability to transcription errors, multilingual settings, non-lexical vocalizations, and real-time interaction. These robustness dimensions are not evaluated.

Despite enabling speaker-controlled speech generation, the paper does not discuss voice impersonation, consent, dataset governance, or misuse safeguards. Overall, the idea and empirical signals are promising, but the missing controlled evidence and evaluation ambiguities leave it marginally below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: reducing the speech–text sequence-length mismatch in joint spoken language modeling.
The proposed text-conditioned cross-attention aggregator is conceptually simple, and producing one speech representation per text token makes downstream joint modeling convenient.
The empirical study covers reconstruction, continuation, acoustic and semantic selection benchmarks, spoken question answering, and both discrete-token and continuous-embedding variants.
A same-training-framework S3-token baseline is included, and the reported results suggest that TASTE may be more effective than this baseline for semantic continuation and StoryCloze.
weaknesses: The reconstruction comparison is fundamentally confounded. TASTE's decoder receives the ground-truth transcript and a separate speaker embedding, whereas codec baselines are expected to reconstruct from their codes. The reported approximately 150-bps rate apparently excludes this side information. Consequently, the headline claim of unusually high-quality reconstruction at extremely low bitrate is not supported by a like-for-like rate–distortion comparison.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed mechanism. There are no controlled ablations for text alignment, token rate, cross-attention design, Whisper layer choice, word-level averaging, quantization depth, or transcript quality. Comparing only against a poorly performing S3 setup cannot establish that mitigating length mismatch is responsible for the gains.

The main comparisons mix different base LMs, parameter counts, training corpora, objectives, decoders, and adaptation regimes. TASTE uses roughly 40,600 hours of training audio, but matched-data and matched-backbone baselines are largely absent. This makes the broad claims of outperforming pretrained SLMs difficult to interpret.

The human continuation advantage over the cascade baseline is very small relative to the reported dispersion (4.16 versus 4.00, with standard deviations around 1.2), yet the paper claims significant superiority without hypothesis tests or confidence intervals. Human evaluation uses only 20 samples per method, and worker screening, compensation, agreement, and quality-control procedures are not reported.

The GPT-4o continuation score is computed after ASR transcription and with a single underspecified judge configuration, conflating generation quality with ASR errors and judge variability. The acoustic metrics are also learned predictors, several of which rate synthesized outputs above the ground truth, so they should not be treated as conclusive evidence of perceptual quality.

The speech-editing evidence is essentially qualitative and focuses on a selected duration example. No systematic evaluation demonstrates controllable transfer of duration, tone, emotion, or other claimed paralinguistic attributes, nor is content leakage or speaker leakage assessed.

The method depends on an ASR transcript and word grouping, so it is not an autonomous speech tokenizer in the usual sense. Robustness to ASR errors, disfluencies, punctuation, non-lexical vocalizations, and out-of-domain speech is not evaluated, despite being central to practical use.

Important implementation details are missing, including aggregator and decoder architecture, loss weights, shallow-layer selection, token-fusion weights, sampling procedures, likelihood computation for the embedding model, and exact training duration for the SLM. The claimed code, model, and demo links are blank in the manuscript, substantially limiting reproducibility.

Equation 7 appears technically inconsistent: for a Gaussian parameterized by variance σ², the KL term should contain σ², whereas the displayed expression contains σ while also using log σ². The use and motivation of a straight-through estimator for the sampled continuous latent are also insufficiently explained.

The evaluation is English-only and largely centered on read speech. The paper does not adequately discuss privacy, consent, copyright, voice-cloning misuse, or demographic bias arising from 40,000 hours of web-collected speech and speaker-conditioned synthesis.

strengths: The paper identifies an important obstacle in joint speech-text modeling: the large sequence-length mismatch between conventional speech tokens and text tokens. Aligning speech representations directly to text positions is a clear and practically useful formulation.

TASTE is technically intuitive and well motivated. Cross-attention from text queries to frozen Whisper representations provides a clean way to obtain variable-rate, text-aligned speech tokens without explicit forced alignment during tokenization.

The reconstruction results are strong: at a reported bitrate of approximately 150 bps, TASTE achieves high predicted speech quality, competitive speaker similarity, and a MUSHRA score close to substantially higher-bitrate systems.

The downstream evaluation covers complementary dimensions, including speech continuation, acoustic consistency, narrative semantics, and spoken question answering. TASLM substantially improves over the matched S3-token baseline and is competitive with considerably larger spoken language models.

The text-aligned editing demonstration provides useful qualitative evidence that the representation captures localized paralinguistic information. The appendix also supplies training details, evaluation prompts, disaggregated benchmark results, and standard deviations.
weaknesses: The bitrate comparison is not fully apples-to-apples. TASTE reconstruction additionally requires the transcript and a speaker embedding, but their transmission costs are excluded, while conventional codec baselines operate from speech alone. Thus, describing TASTE as a roughly 150-bps codec or claiming an extreme advantage over codecs is potentially misleading without reporting total side-information cost or clearly framing the task as transcript-conditioned resynthesis.

The empirical analysis lacks ablations for the central design choices: last-layer keys versus other layers, shallow-layer values, text-conditioned attention, word-level averaging, RVQ depth, discrete versus continuous representations, and reconstruction training. Consequently, the results establish that the complete system works but do not isolate why it works or substantiate the claimed mechanism.

Dependence on ASR transcription is underexamined. Experiments appear to use clean or provided transcripts, with no analysis of recognition errors, noisy speech, accents, disfluencies, punctuation, or tokenization failures. This limits evidence for robustness in realistic spoken-language settings.

The human evaluations use only 20 samples per method. Although multiple judgments are collected, the paper provides no confidence intervals, paired significance tests, rater-quality controls, or demographic information. Some claimed advantages, such as the human-MOS improvement over the matched cascade, are small relative to the reported variation.

Several downstream comparisons are confounded by different base models, parameter counts, training data, and adaptation procedures. The matched S3 baseline is valuable, but stronger controlled baselines—such as length-reduced/interleaved tokens trained with the same LLM, data, and budget—are needed to show that text alignment itself causes the gains.

The mathematical and reproducibility descriptions need tightening. In particular, the stated KL expression appears inconsistent about whether sigma denotes variance or standard deviation, the RVQ objective omits implementation details such as stop-gradient/codebook updates, and the spoken-LM training schedule and inference settings are incomplete. The promised code/demo links are blank in the submitted PDF.

The paper does not discuss misuse risks associated with speech generation, speaker imitation, or localized prosody transfer, nor safeguards or the privacy/licensing implications of the large web-sourced speech corpus. This is a notable omission for a generative speech system.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant idea: use transcript-token queries to aggregate speech representations into a one-to-one text-aligned sequence, substantially reducing sequence length and simplifying joint text-speech prediction.

TASTE achieves strong reconstruction results at a very low reported token rate, with evaluation covering intelligibility, perceptual quality, duration consistency, speaker similarity, and human judgments.

The experimental scope is broad, including speech continuation, SALMON, StoryCloze, spoken question answering, speech editing, noise robustness, ASR sensitivity, attention visualization, and component ablations.

The comparison against an S3-token model using the same LLaMA-3.2 base provides some evidence that tokenization design matters: TASTE produces large improvements in continuation and semantic-selection performance while tuning only about 45M parameters.
The paper is generally well organized, includes useful implementation and human-evaluation details in the appendix, acknowledges important deployment risks, and discusses several limitations.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not adequately isolate the benefit of the proposed learned tokenizer. There is no matched baseline using simple word-level pooling, attention resampling, forced-alignment pooling, or another text-aligned transformation of S3/Whisper features. The direct S3 baseline is near chance on several tasks, so it is unclear whether TASTE is intrinsically superior or merely avoids an especially unsuitable length-mismatched modeling setup.

The reported bitrate comparison with standalone neural codecs is potentially misleading. TASTE reconstruction additionally requires the transcript and a speaker embedding, whose information costs are not clearly included. Consequently, claims of high-end reconstruction at approximately 150 bps are not directly comparable to codecs that reconstruct from their bitstreams alone.

Comparisons with published SLMs are substantially confounded by different base LMs, parameter counts, training corpora, tokenizers, and decoding procedures. TASLM is notably worse than Spirit LM Expressive on SALMON, especially for room and background attributes, while the reported overall score averages heterogeneous benchmarks in an arguably arbitrary way.

The human evaluation is too small for strong headline conclusions: only 20 samples per method are selected, no significance tests or confidence intervals over system differences are reported, and the displayed sample-level deviations are large. The so-called MUSHRA evaluation omits the standard low-pass anchor, while continuation judgments mix intelligibility, naturalness, and semantic coherence into one underspecified score.

GPT-4o evaluation depends on ASR transcripts and an incompletely specified external model configuration. The near tie with the matched cascade system (3.16 versus 3.15) does not substantiate a meaningful semantic advantage, and no uncertainty or repeated-judge analysis is supplied.

Important reproducibility details remain missing, including the precise Whisper variant, aggregator and unit-decoder architectures, loss weights, SLM training length, LoRA target modules, sampling parameters, and random-seed variability. The promised code/model/demo link is blank in the submitted manuscript.

There is a technical inconsistency in the latent-modeling objective: Equation 7 appears to use sigma rather than sigma squared in the Gaussian KL term. It is unclear whether this is only a typographical error or reflects the implementation.

Evidence that the representation specifically preserves paralinguistic information is limited. Speaker similarity and one duration-swapping example do not establish broad retention or controllability of prosody, emotion, pitch, speaking style, or non-lexical events.

The method relies on ASR transcripts and offline cross-attention over speech, limiting streaming use, multilingual generalization, treatment of ASR failures, and speech without clean lexical content. These constraints narrow the significance of the otherwise promising approach.

strengths: The idea of learning text-aligned, low-rate speech representations specifically for joint text-speech modeling is intuitive and potentially useful.
The method is clearly motivated and combines a frozen ASR encoder, cross-attention aggregation, residual quantization, and reconstruction training in a reasonably coherent design.

The paper evaluates several dimensions, including reconstruction, continuation, likelihood-based benchmarks, spoken question answering, noise robustness, and discrete versus continuous representations.

TASTE obtains strong conditional reconstruction results at a low speech-token rate and notably strong StoryCloze and speech-continuation scores. The appendices provide useful ASR, representation-layer, and noise ablations.
The paper acknowledges important scope and misuse limitations and includes an ethics discussion.
weaknesses: The headline bitrate comparison is not apples-to-apples. TASTE is a conditional codec requiring a transcript during both encoding and reconstruction, yet its approximately 150 bps figure excludes the text side information and apparently the speaker embedding. It is compared against standalone codecs that must encode lexical content themselves, substantially overstating the compression advantage.

The experiments do not isolate the central claim that text alignment itself improves spoken language modeling. There is no matched-rate alternative using forced alignment, CTC pooling, a learned resampler, or another text-conditioned codec. The main same-training baseline uses 25 Hz S3 tokens and therefore differs drastically in sequence rate and alignment structure. Module ablations report only an S3 reconstruction proxy rather than downstream SLM performance.

Comparisons with prior SLMs are heavily confounded by different base language models, training corpora, tokenizers, optimization, and decoding procedures. Training TASTE on roughly 40,600 hours while comparing against published systems does not support attributing gains specifically to the proposed tokenization.

Several conclusions overstate the results. On SALMON, both TASLM variants trail Spirit LM Expr. and the token model also trails TWIST-7B; the overall likelihood advantage over Spirit LM Expr. is small. The cascade and TASLM continuation scores are also extremely close relative to the reported variability, despite claims that TASLM surpasses its corresponding text pipeline.

The human evaluation is too small for the strength of the claims: only 20 samples per method are used, no significance tests or confidence intervals are reported, and the MUSHRA study omits the standard low-quality anchor. Reported per-sample standard deviations do not establish statistically reliable differences. Generation settings and evaluator-quality controls are insufficiently documented.

Claims that the representation preserves essential paralinguistic information are only partially supported. Quantitative evidence mainly covers speaker similarity and duration; pitch, intonation, emotion, speaking style, and non-lexical information are not systematically evaluated. Speech editing is demonstrated primarily through one duration-focused example without a controlled perceptual study.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a large experimental paper. The manuscript does not specify the Whisper variant, aggregator and decoder architectures, SLM training duration or number of updates, sampling parameters, dataset filtering, or complete evaluation sample counts. The stated code/model link is absent from the manuscript.

The continuous-embedding objective is technically ambiguous: the text defines sampling with standard deviation sigma, but the stated KL expression appears to use sigma rather than sigma squared. More generally, the behavior and stability of this stochastic formulation are not ablated.

Dependence on accurate transcripts materially limits the claimed generality to spontaneous, multilingual, overlapping, non-lexical, or low-resource speech. The English read-speech-centered evaluation does not establish that the approach works in the broader spoken-language settings used to motivate it.

strengths: TASTE presents a clear and useful idea: conditioning speech-token extraction on the transcript to produce one-to-one text-aligned acoustic tokens, substantially simplifying joint text-speech autoregressive modeling.

The empirical scope is strong. The paper evaluates reconstruction quality, continuation, acoustic and semantic likelihood benchmarks, spoken question answering, editing, noise robustness, ASR sensitivity, and several architectural choices.

The approximately 3 Hz representation achieves an appealing quality-efficiency tradeoff. It retains duration and speaker information far better than the text-only baseline while remaining much more compact than conventional codecs.

The spoken-language-modeling results are promising: the 1B TASLM variants substantially improve over the matched S3-token baseline and are competitive with much larger pretrained SLMs, especially on continuation and StoryCloze.

The paper includes useful supplementary evidence, including per-task results, standard deviations, attention visualizations, human evaluation instructions, training details, limitations, and an appropriate discussion of voice-manipulation risks.
weaknesses: Several comparisons are not fully controlled. Competing SLMs use different base language models, training data, parameter-update regimes, and tokenizers, so the results do not isolate whether the gains arise from TASTE itself. A matched alternative using the same base LM, data, compute, and several strong alignment/interleaving strategies is needed.

The low-bitrate reconstruction comparison is not entirely apples-to-apples: TASTE relies on text and a global speaker embedding, whereas several codec baselines reconstruct from their bitstreams alone. The accounting and claims should explicitly include or separately report all side information.

The central claim that TASTE isolates paralinguistic information is only partially established. Duration swapping and reconstruction metrics are suggestive, but controlled probes for prosody, emotion, pitch, speaker identity, and residual lexical leakage would provide much stronger support.

Human evaluation uses only 20 utterances per method, reports no confidence intervals or significance tests over system-level differences, and omits important annotator-quality-control details. The MUSHRA-like evaluation also lacks the standard low-pass anchor, limiting confidence in small perceptual differences.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the stated release: the manuscript shows no usable code/model URL and omits important details such as exact component architectures, several loss weights, SLM training duration, LoRA target modules, and decoding settings. Some equations are also ambiguous, notably the variance term in the KL loss and the precise RVQ commitment-loss implementation.

The method inherently depends on reliable lexical transcripts and word grouping, limiting applicability to non-lexical sounds, overlapping speakers, code-switching, and poorly recognized speech. Noise experiments are helpful, but do not fully address these broader conditions.
